name: SingleFile. Aliases and forms: the SingleFile web extension (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge and others), single-file-cli (the command-line/Node form driving a headless browser), single-file-core (the embeddable library), and SingleFileZ (a ZIP-based self-extracting variant). Author: Gildas Lormeau. Predecessors and alternatives in the same niche: browser Save Page As (Complete), MHTML/MAF, Save Page WE, Web Archive (webarchive) format, and the WARC-based tools covered in item 2. Distinct from the extraction tools in this research set: SingleFile aims at VISUAL FIDELITY of a rendered page, not at content extraction.
kind: Library plus browser extension plus CLI tool. Not a standard, benchmark, service or regulation. Its output format is plain HTML with everything inlined, which is its own de-facto interchange convention rather than a specified one.
maturity: Production and actively maintained, with a long release history and a large user base; it is the de-facto standard for single-file page capture and is used as the capture backend by several downstream projects and archiving workflows. The shadow-DOM and canvas handling have improved materially over successive releases (constructed stylesheets of closed shadow roots are no longer lost in recent versions; a canvas tainted by a cross-origin resource is now reported rather than silently dropped), which is a good signal about the project's attitude to silent failure. There is no specification and no versioned output contract, so the output format is whatever the current release emits.
license: AGPL-3.0, with a commercial licence available on request. THIS IS A MATERIAL CONSTRAINT AND IS EASY TO MISS. AGPL's network clause means that if SingleFile code (including single-file-core) is incorporated into a system and that system is made available to users over a network, the complete corresponding source of the combined work must be offered. For a purely local research tool with no network service, the practical obligation is limited; for anything exposed as a service, it is significant. This is the strictest licence in this research set and it should be checked against the project's intentions before any code is vendored. Using SingleFile as an external CLI process rather than linking its library is the usual way to avoid the combined-work question, and even that should be considered deliberately rather than assumed safe. [uncertain] on the precise boundary as applied to a particular integration -- this is a legal judgement, not a technical one.
keeps_and_discards: SingleFile keeps the RENDERED page as a self-contained artifact: it walks the live DOM after scripts have run, inlines stylesheets, images, fonts, SVGs and iframe contents as data URIs or inline content, serialises canvas elements to their image representation where permitted, and writes the result as one HTML file with no external dependencies. It DISCARDS scripts by default -- the saved file is inert, which is the point, since the goal is a document that renders identically without executing anything. That single choice defines the tool: what is kept is the RESULT of the page's behaviour at capture time, and what is lost is the behaviour itself. Concretely also discarded or unreliable: canvas and video content when CORS taints the element (the tool states it is sometimes unable to save the image representation of canvas and snapshots of video elements, for security reasons); sandboxed iframe contents on Firefox, which the browser does not permit reading; external resources for pages loaded from the filesystem; and all form-control property state (typed values, checkedness after interaction), since serialisation writes attributes and not IDL properties. Compared with the getHTML approach of item 26, SingleFile keeps strictly more (subresources, canvas pixels, computed styling) and is strictly heavier; compared with a WARC capture (item 2) it keeps a rendered snapshot rather than the HTTP exchange.
structure_preserved: The DOM structure is preserved essentially exactly, since the tool serialises the live tree. Shadow boundaries are preserved -- this is one of SingleFile's genuinely strong points and it has improved over time, including handling of constructed stylesheets attached to shadow roots. iframes are inlined, which FLATTENS a document boundary into the parent document: structurally faithful for rendering, structurally lossy as a record, because the fact that content came from a separate browsing context with a separate origin is not recoverable from the output in the way it is from a WARC. Styling is preserved by inlining and by rewriting, which means the CASCADE is partly resolved into the artifact rather than preserved as authored -- a saved page's CSS is not the site's CSS. Tabular relations, nesting and order all survive. What has no representation is anything that was never in the DOM: CSS generated content is rendered by the browser from rules that ARE inlined, so it survives as a rule rather than as text and re-renders correctly, which is actually better than any DOM-text extractor manages.
interactive_elements: Controls survive as markup and are visually intact but functionally dead: scripts are removed, so buttons do nothing, menus do not open, and any content that would have been revealed by interaction is absent unless it happened to be in the DOM at capture time. Links remain navigable to the live web. For an agent or a sensor this is the decisive limitation -- a SingleFile capture is a photograph of one interaction state, and the affordance inventory it preserves is markup-level (what elements exist and what attributes they carry) rather than behavioural. That is adequate for recording what affordances a page presented and useless for exercising them.
interactive_state_fidelity: Attribute-level state survives (disabled, aria-*, open on details, the checked and selected ATTRIBUTES as authored); property-backed state does not (input.value as typed, checkedness after interaction, selectedness, indeterminate, files), for the same attribute-versus-property reason set out in item 26. So a capture of a half-completed form shows an empty form. There is a nuance worth noting: because SingleFile captures after scripts have run, any state a framework has REFLECTED into attributes or into the DOM is captured, which on a modern component-based page is often most of the meaningful state -- so the practical fidelity is better than the raw attribute/property split suggests, and worse than a naive reading of 'it saves the rendered page' implies. Token cost is not a relevant axis: SingleFile output is not intended for a model and is enormous.
layout_awareness: Layout-aware throughout, and unavoidably so. SingleFile reads computed styles to decide what to inline and how to rewrite rules, it captures the rendered state of canvas elements, and its whole success criterion is that the saved file LOOKS like the original. It also performs behaviours aimed at getting more of the page into view before capture -- lazy-loaded image handling requires provoking or resolving the page's own loading logic, which is a rendering-and-viewport-dependent operation. There is no layout-free mode and there could not be. In this project's terms it is entirely on the actuator side of the line.
javascript_required: Yes, emphatically, and in both directions. The page's scripts must have run for the capture to be meaningful (that is the tool's advantage over fetching HTML), and SingleFile's own code runs in the page context or via the extension APIs to walk the DOM and fetch subresources. The saved output, by contrast, contains no scripts and requires none. The consequence that matters for a sensor: capturing with SingleFile means the page is fully live and its telemetry has fired, and the capture itself issues additional network requests for every subresource it needs to inline -- which is a substantially larger network footprint than reading the DOM.
evaluation_method: There is no published evaluation. Correctness is established by visual inspection and by a large user base reporting regressions -- an issue tracker and a maintained known-issues list, which is real but informal quality assurance. No corpus, no metric, no comparison against alternatives has been published by the author or by anyone else as far as this research found. The honest statement is that SingleFile's fidelity claim rests on reputation and on the absence of complaints, not on measurement. The evaluation that WOULD be informative and is straightforward: capture N pages, re-open each capture and the live page side by side at a fixed viewport, and compare rendered output pixel-wise or structurally; separately, compare the capture's DOM against the live DOM node-for-node to quantify what the serialisation dropped. Neither has been published.
corpus_size_and_origins: No evaluation corpus exists. The de-facto corpus is the aggregate of what users have saved, which is large and completely uncharacterised -- unknown size, unknown origin distribution, unknown archetype mix, and observable only through the bugs it produced. This is a common and under-remarked situation for widely-used tools: enormous real-world exposure, zero published measurement. Any claim that SingleFile achieves high fidelity is an inference from its popularity, and should be labelled as such. [uncertain] throughout this field by construction.
reported_precision_recall: None published, and none is really definable for a visual-fidelity tool without choosing a metric first. The relevant known deficiencies are qualitative and are documented by the author in the known-issues file rather than quantified: canvas image representation and video snapshots are sometimes unsavable due to CORS; Firefox cannot save the contents of sandboxed iframes; external resources are not embedded for pages loaded from the filesystem; certain browser-store and Mozilla domains cannot be captured at all because extensions are blocked there; and a duplicate-image grouping option can fail on reopening. The project's own measured position in this research set -- a capture holding 99.7% of a page's affordances against a projection drawing 80.9% -- is the kind of number that does not exist for SingleFile, which means the project has better fidelity measurement of its own capture than the most widely-used capture tool has of itself.
independent_oracle: None in the tool. Two are available and cheap. (1) RE-RENDER COMPARISON: open the capture and the live page at an identical viewport and compare, which uses the browser itself as an oracle independent of SingleFile's serialisation logic. (2) DOM COMPARISON: parse the capture and diff its node tree against the live DOM the capture was taken from, which isolates serialisation loss from rendering loss. The second is the more useful for a structured pipeline and it is what any project relying on SingleFile output should run. The tool's own improvement of reporting rather than silently dropping a CORS-tainted canvas is a step toward self-oracling and is the right direction.
evidence_independence: Not applicable in the usual sense, because there is no evidence to be independent about -- no vendor benchmarks, no author-run comparisons, no third-party evaluations located. That is worth recording explicitly: SingleFile is widely described as producing a faithful copy, and that description originates with the project itself and is repeated without measurement everywhere it appears. It is a reputation, not a finding. No figures should be quoted for SingleFile fidelity because none exist.
page_archetype_coverage: Unmeasured; the failure modes suggest the spread. Article, documentation and forum archetypes should capture near-perfectly, being static DOM plus images. Product and media-rich pages are where canvas, video and CORS-tainted resources bite, so fidelity degrades in exactly the archetypes where visual content carries the most meaning. Application-shell and dashboard archetypes capture as a dead snapshot of one state, which is nearly worthless for a page whose content is behind interaction. Listing pages with infinite scroll capture only what has been loaded, so the capture's completeness depends on how far the operator scrolled before invoking the tool -- an operator-dependent and unrecorded variable that silently determines what the artifact contains.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Script-neutral for content: serialisation preserves code points and the inlined stylesheets carry whatever fonts the page used, so CJK and RTL pages capture correctly provided the fonts are embeddable. The one locale-adjacent behaviour documented is in FILENAME generation, where special characters (~, +, ?, %, *, :, |, quote, angle brackets, backslash) are replaced with full-width equivalents to keep filesystem compatibility, and other invalid characters become underscores -- a small but instructive detail, since it means the capture's identity in the filesystem is a lossy transform of the page title and cannot be relied upon as a key. Font embedding is where non-Latin scripts can degrade: a page relying on a system font for CJK will have nothing to embed and will re-render with whatever the viewer's system provides. [uncertain] -- no measurement of non-Latin capture fidelity was located.
leaks_outward: Substantial and under-appreciated, and it is the sharpest contrast with a DOM-read approach. To inline subresources, SingleFile FETCHES them -- every image, stylesheet, font, iframe and media file must be retrieved, which means the capture generates a burst of network requests to the origin and to every third-party host the page references. Those requests announce the capture: they are timed differently from normal page loading, they may re-request resources already cached, and they reach hosts (ad networks, CDNs, analytics) that then learn a second retrieval occurred. Combined with the requirement that the page be fully live, a SingleFile capture is one of the most network-visible operations in this research set. For a project whose fidelity evidence rests on a corpus where 75% of pages fetch live resources on every read, this is also the mechanism by which that happens.
mechanism_detectability: Moderate to high, and higher than the alternatives. Three channels. (1) The subresource re-fetch burst described above is directly observable server-side and has a recognisable shape. (2) SingleFile runs as an extension in the page's context for some operations, and extension presence is detectable by several well-known techniques (injected elements, timing, accessible web resources); the tool also manipulates the page to resolve lazy-loaded content, and any DOM manipulation is visible to the page's own MutationObserver. (3) The capture takes noticeable wall-clock time on a large page, which is timeable. None of this matters for the tool's intended use -- a user saving a page they are reading -- and all of it matters for a covert sensor. The verdict for this project is clear: SingleFile is not a stealth capture mechanism and should not be used as one.
countermeasures: For the tool's own robustness: it degrades gracefully on CORS-tainted canvas by reporting rather than dropping, which is the right behaviour and worth copying. For a user wanting a quieter capture there is no configuration that removes the subresource fetching, because the fetching IS the feature. A project needing both fidelity and quietness has to split the problem: read the DOM without fetching (item 26) for the structural record, and accept that subresource content is only obtainable by requesting it. That split should be a deliberate architectural decision rather than an accident of which tool was convenient.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not measured by anyone. The interesting unmeasured quantity for this project is the reverse of the usual one: what does SingleFile capture that a getHTML serialisation does NOT, expressed as content rather than as bytes? The answer is subresource content (images, fonts, media), canvas pixels, and resolved styling -- none of which a text-oriented fold uses. So for a fold that reads text, structure and affordances, the marginal fidelity SingleFile buys over a plain DOM serialisation is close to zero, while its cost in network exposure, detectability and artifact size is very high. That comparison, which nobody has published, is the decisive one for this project and it argues against adoption for the read path.
gate_state_at_capture: Not recorded, and SingleFile is unusually exposed to the problem because it captures whatever is on screen. A capture taken with a consent banner displayed contains the banner; one taken behind a paywall contains the paywall; one taken while logged in contains personalised content. None of this is annotated in the output. Since the tool is invoked manually by a user at a moment of their choosing, the gate state is entirely an artefact of when the button was pressed, and the artifact carries no record of it. For corpus construction this is the silent-mixing hazard in its purest form.
determinism: Not deterministic in practice, for reasons that are mostly the page's fault rather than the tool's. The capture depends on when it was taken relative to the page's own asynchronous work, on how far the operator scrolled, on which lazy resources had loaded, on animation phase, on viewport size, and on which subresource fetches succeeded. Two captures of the same URL seconds apart differ. The serialisation logic itself is deterministic given a fixed DOM and a fixed set of successfully fetched resources. There is also no canonicalisation of attribute order or of data-URI encoding, so byte-level comparison of two captures is not meaningful even when the content is identical.
determinism_across_versions: Output drifts with SingleFile releases -- the shadow-root and canvas handling changed materially over time, so a 2023 capture and a 2026 capture of the same page differ in what they contain, not merely in formatting -- and with browser version, since the DOM being serialised and the computed styles being read both change. There is no output format version stamped in the artifact as far as this research found, which makes it hard to know retrospectively which behaviour produced a given file. Any archive built on SingleFile should record the tool version and the browser build alongside each capture; nothing forces this.
reproducibility: The ARTIFACT is highly reproducible in the sense that matters most for archiving: a saved file is self-contained, has no external dependencies, opens in any browser years later, and renders the same because it carries its own resources. That is a genuine and substantial strength and it is why the tool is used for archiving. What is NOT reproducible is the ACT of capture -- re-running it later against the same URL produces a different file, and there is no way to re-derive a capture from anything other than the capture. So SingleFile freezes well and cannot be re-obtained, which is the same posture as a photograph.
failure_modes: From the maintained known-issues list and from the mechanism. (1) CORS-TAINTED CANVAS AND VIDEO -- the image representation cannot be read, so the capture has a blank or missing region where visual content was; now reported rather than silently dropped, which is the right handling. (2) SANDBOXED IFRAMES on Firefox cannot be read, so their content is absent. (3) FILESYSTEM-LOADED PAGES do not embed their external resources. (4) BROWSER-STORE AND CERTAIN VENDOR DOMAINS cannot be captured at all because extensions are blocked there. (5) SCRIPT REMOVAL means anything behind interaction is absent -- the largest functional limitation and inherent to the design. (6) LAZY-LOADED CONTENT below the point the operator scrolled to is simply not there. (7) FORM PROPERTY STATE is lost. (8) SUBRESOURCE FETCH FAILURES produce a capture with missing pieces, and whether this is reported depends on the resource type. (9) ARTIFACT SIZE on media-heavy pages, since every image becomes a base64 data URI with roughly a third of size overhead. (10) Filename mangling of special characters, which breaks any assumption that the filename identifies the page.
failure_visibility: Better than most and improving, which deserves credit. The project explicitly changed behaviour so that a canvas tainted by a cross-origin resource is REPORTED rather than dropped silently, and the extension surfaces a progress and log UI during capture. But the visibility is aimed at a human watching a capture happen, not at a downstream consumer of the artifact: the saved file itself does not carry a machine-readable manifest of what failed to embed, what was skipped, or how far the page had loaded. For a pipeline, that means the silent-degradation problem is only partly solved -- the human sees the warning and the artifact does not carry it. A project using SingleFile output would need to capture the log alongside the file and treat the pair as the artifact.
scale_limits: Cost is dominated by subresource fetching and by base64 encoding, both linear in resource volume but with large constants, and by the resulting artifact size -- a media-rich page can produce a file of many megabytes, and base64 inflates every binary resource by about a third. Capture time on a large page is seconds, not milliseconds. The CLI form drives a headless browser per page, so throughput for bulk capture is bounded by browser instances rather than by anything about the serialisation. For an archive, storage grows at roughly the page's full resource weight per capture with no deduplication across captures -- the same image saved on a hundred pages is stored a hundred times, which is a real and unaddressed scaling problem and one that content-addressed storage (item 3 of the adjacent set, Merkle DAG and content addressing) solves directly.
delta_cost_model: None whatsoever, and this is the clearest structural mismatch with this project. SingleFile is a whole-page, from-scratch operation: every capture walks the entire DOM, re-fetches every subresource, and writes a complete new file. There is no incremental mode, no diffing between captures, and no reuse of previously-captured resources across captures. Cost is O(page + all resources) every time. What falls outside any notional per-change cost, stated for completeness: everything -- the DOM walk, the subresource fetches, the base64 encoding, and the file write are all O(page), and nothing in the design is change-aware. The only incrementality available is at the storage layer, by content-addressing the inlined resources so repeated captures share them, and that requires abandoning the single-file format that is the tool's entire point. VERDICT: SingleFile and O(delta) are architecturally incompatible; it is a snapshot tool.
reanchoring_stability: No addressing scheme at all -- the artifact is an HTML file and nodes within it have no assigned identity, so re-anchoring across two captures of the same page means diffing two DOMs with no help from the tool. Because iframes are inlined and styling is rewritten, the capture's DOM is not identical to the live DOM it came from, so addresses computed against the live page do not necessarily resolve against the capture. That is a genuine hazard for any pipeline that captures with SingleFile and addresses with xpaths: the two trees differ in ways the tool does not document. If a capture is to be addressable, addresses must be computed at capture time from the live DOM, not later from the file.
adversarial_exposure: SingleFile preserves everything in the DOM regardless of visibility, and additionally preserves the CSS that conceals it -- so a saved page contains both the hidden content and the rules hiding it, which is actually the most complete adversarial record of any capture method here: an analyst can re-render it and can also inspect the concealment mechanism, because both are in the artifact. That is a real advantage for FORENSICS and a corresponding hazard for CONSUMPTION, since anything that extracts text from a SingleFile capture inherits every concealed payload. Because the capture is a rendered snapshot, it also captures script-injected content that a fetched HTML copy would miss, including dynamically-inserted injections. Two specific hazards. First, the capture is inert HTML but it is still HTML: opening one in a browser with scripting enabled is safe only because scripts were removed, and any pipeline that reparses a capture and re-enables scripting, or that uses an unsafe parse path, reintroduces the risk. Second, data URIs in the artifact can carry arbitrary content and are a well-known vector for smuggling payloads past naive scanners -- a capture is a large blob of base64 that most content filters will not inspect.
provenance_carrying: Weak. The output is an HTML file; the tool inserts a comment with the source URL and capture timestamp, which is genuine provenance but is document-level and easily lost or edited. There is no per-node provenance, no record of which inlined resource came from which origin (a critical loss, since inlining erases the third-party boundary entirely -- an image from an ad network and an image from the site become indistinguishable data URIs), no shadow-depth marking beyond the DOM structure itself, and no gate-state record. The erasure of the origin boundary during inlining is the most significant provenance loss and it is inherent to the format: a self-contained file cannot, by construction, tell you where its pieces came from unless it records it separately, and SingleFile does not.
roundtrip_safety: Not designed for round-tripping and not a fixed point. Re-capturing a SingleFile capture with SingleFile produces a different file (resources already inlined get re-processed, styling is re-resolved). Parsing and re-serialising a capture with a standard HTML serialiser will not reproduce it byte-identically because attribute order and data-URI formatting are not canonicalised. There is no escaping policy documented; the tool relies on the browser's own serialisation for HTML escaping, and the mutation-XSS hardening in Element.getHTML (item 26) is the relevant modern concern for any pipeline that reparses saved markup. A useful weaker check does exist and is unpublished: capture, reopen the capture, capture again, and compare the two artifacts' DOM trees -- differences localise serialisation instability.
token_budget_and_ordering: Not a model-facing format and should never be given to one. A SingleFile artifact is HTML with every stylesheet inlined and every image as a base64 data URI, so it is the most token-expensive representation of a page that exists -- routinely megabytes, most of it base64 that carries no linguistic content and tokenises terribly. Its role, if any, is as a frozen source artifact from which a text projection is computed offline. If it is used that way, the data URIs must be stripped before any tokenisation, which is trivial but must not be forgotten.
representation_cost: Very high per page: the full weight of the page's resources plus roughly 33% base64 overhead, with no cross-capture deduplication. What is bought per byte is visual fidelity and offline self-containment; what is bought for a text-oriented pipeline is essentially nothing beyond what a DOM serialisation already provides. That asymmetry is the core cost finding for this project.
what_could_be_adopted: Three things, none of them the tool itself. (1) THE REPORT-DON'T-DROP DISCIPLINE, exemplified by the change to report a CORS-tainted canvas rather than silently omitting it. This is precisely the anti-silent-degradation stance the project holds, arrived at independently by a production tool through user pain, and it should be generalised: every resource or subtree that could not be captured produces a record, not an absence. (2) THE SELF-CONTAINED-ARTIFACT PRINCIPLE for reproducibility -- a capture that carries everything it needs can be re-opened years later without the live web, which is the property item 23's orphan study and item 25's change-detection literature both independently identify as the missing ingredient. The project should have an equivalent frozen artifact even if it is not a single HTML file; a getHTML string plus an address-keyed resource table achieves the same end with far less weight and preserves the origin boundary that inlining destroys. (3) THE KNOWN-ISSUES LIST AS A PUBLISHED LIMITATION SET -- SingleFile maintains an explicit, public enumeration of what it cannot capture, which is exactly the declared-incompleteness practice recommended throughout this research set, and it is notable that the most widely-used capture tool does this while none of the extraction libraries do. Explicitly NOT to be adopted: SingleFile as the project's capture mechanism, for four independent reasons -- AGPL licensing, subresource re-fetching that is both detectable and network-noisy, no incremental mode of any kind, and a format whose inlining erases exactly the per-origin provenance the design depends on.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS. SingleFile makes no content judgements, names no regions, and classifies nothing; it serialises what is there. It has optional user-driven content removal (highlight, annotate, remove) but that is manual editing, not an automatic heuristic. No violation. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY. The tool reads computed styles and captures rendered canvas by design, and its success criterion is visual. There is no layout-free mode. If used at all it belongs beside the screenshot and the ASCII wireframe, as a visual-fidelity artifact, never as the fold's substrate. o_delta: REJECTED. There is no incremental capture, no diffing, no resource reuse across captures; every capture is O(page plus all subresources) including a full network re-fetch. This is architecturally incompatible with an incremental sensor and no configuration changes it. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- it runs a real browser against a real page and there is nothing stubbed. The caution is on the EVIDENCE side rather than the mechanism: SingleFile's fidelity is entirely unmeasured, so any claim built on 'we captured it with SingleFile so it is faithful' is an appeal to reputation, and the tool's own known-issues list enumerates real gaps. Treat its fidelity as NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY until measured locally. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: REQUIRES SCRUTINY AND IS THE ITEM'S SHARPEST CONSTRAINT QUESTION. Recent releases state that constructed stylesheets of CLOSED shadow roots are no longer lost, which means the tool reaches inside closed roots. As an extension it has access the page does not, so this need not involve patching attachShadow -- but the project cannot verify by inspection which mechanism is used, and a design that refuses to defeat the closed-root boundary should not adopt a component that may defeat it by other means. VERDICT: REJECTED pending verification of the mechanism; and even if the mechanism is a privileged extension API rather than a patch, reaching closed-root content violates the SPIRIT of the constraint as stated in item 28 -- the constraint is about the boundary, not the technique. OVERALL VERDICT: rejected as a capture mechanism on four grounds (AGPL, network detectability, no incrementality, provenance-erasing inlining) plus an unresolved closed-shadow-root question; adopt only its report-don't-drop discipline, its self-contained-artifact principle in a lighter form, and its practice of publishing an explicit limitation set.
governance_signal_handling: None. SingleFile is a user-invoked tool operating on a page the user is already viewing, so it never consults robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt or AIPREF, and there is no mechanism for it to do so. Its subresource fetching is a real retrieval of third-party resources with no governance check, which is the one place a governance question genuinely arises and is unaddressed -- a capture pulls images and fonts from CDNs and ad networks that may have their own terms. The CLI form used for bulk capture is a crawler in all but name and inherits crawler obligations that the extension form does not; anyone using single-file-cli at scale should treat it as such.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The most exposing capture format in this research set and it should be classified accordingly. A SingleFile artifact is a complete rendered copy of a page as the operator saw it, including all images, all personalised content, and on an authenticated page the operator's own account details, messages and any third-party personal data displayed. Because subresources are inlined, personal data embedded in images (a profile photo, a document scan, a screenshot in a forum post) is carried in the artifact as data URIs, which most scanning and redaction tooling will not inspect. Erasure is straightforward at the file level (delete the file) and impossible at the sub-document level without editing the HTML. Two structural notes: inlining destroys the origin boundary, so an artifact cannot answer 'which of this content came from a third party', which is a question a data-protection assessment may need; and there is no gate-state record, so an archive silently mixes public, consented, paywalled and authenticated captures. Retention classification and gate-state annotation must be added externally. [uncertain] on any specific lawful-basis analysis under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, which is item 19's subject; the AGPL assessment above is likewise a flag for legal review rather than advice.
